records.title: The opening got busy
records.prose: The bark came away and the ants came out everywhere. I kept choosing one to eat. Every time I chose, another walked across my foot. Had to stop choosing.
records.identityEvidence: Adult female. Dark forecrown and black malar stripe support female identification in sources15 and31. Exact age unrecorded.
records.visibleScene: A female pileated woodpecker clings beside a large exposed patch and cavity in a trunk.
records.fictionBoundary: Excavation is visible; ants, their release and the shifting attention are fiction grounded in this species eating ants from excavated wood. No insects are claimed visible.
records.creator: NPS/Christopher Vuille-Kowing

records.title: Half a beak left
records.prose: The black bar rang when I struck it. Shifted half a beak to the left and sank straight into food. I had brought enough force for a tree. Took the next bite with just my tongue.
records.identityEvidence: Adult female. Dark forecrown and black malar stripe support female identification in sources15 and31. Exact age unrecorded.
records.visibleScene: A female pileated woodpecker clings to a wooden suet feeder, holding a crumb at its bill tip beside a black wire grid.
records.fictionBoundary: Feeding, grid, suet and crumb are visible. Prior striking, the sound, sideways adjustment and the following tongue movement are fiction. No injury or brain-shock claim.
records.creator: NPS/Gordon Dietzman

records.title: Paddling the air
records.prose: Put my head down with his. Pushed a little farther. My feet left the water. I came up in a hurry and found him tipped over beside me, paddling air with both feet. Waited for him to come up before I tried again.
records.identityEvidence: Adult male in fiction. Adult appearance is supported; sex is unrecorded in all source photographs.
records.visibleScene: Two American white pelicans tip forward into water with their heads submerged, feet raised and wings partly extended.
records.fictionBoundary: Both tipped bodies and exposed feet are visible. Otis surfacing first, his alarm and waiting are fiction. This is surface upending, not plunge diving.
records.sourceTitle: American white pelicans feeding in the Yellowstone River
records.creator: NPS/Diane Renkin

records.title: An unnecessary circle
records.prose: We touched bills and went on swimming. Every time one of us turned, the other had to turn too. We made a very slow circle. I could have lifted my head.
records.identityEvidence: Adult male in fiction. Adult appearance is supported; sex is unrecorded in all source photographs.
records.visibleScene: Two adult white pelicans swim pressed close, with their long bills aligned and overlapping.
records.fictionBoundary: The close pair and aligned bills are visible. Sustained contact, circling and choosing to remain entangled are fiction. Companion sex and mate status are unrecorded; no courtship act claimed as documentary fact.
records.sourceTitle: Pair of American white pelicans on Yellowstone River
records.creator: NPS/Diane Renkin

records.holdReason: Hold prose: the tiny fish and enormous gape are a good photograph, but the attempted payoff depended on showing off for an observer. That added too little beyond a feeding caption.

records.visibleScene: Two American white pelicans swim; the right bird opens its bill around a small fish.
records.fictionBoundary: Source explicitly identifies the fish. No invented gifting or companion response. This right bird is the avatar subject.
records.sourceTitle: American white pelican in Yellowstone River
records.creator: NPS/Diane Renkin

records.title: Back above the nest
records.prose: Drove the hawk away from my nest. He made a wide circle. I cut across it and drove him away again. We have returned to my nest twice. I am beginning to dislike how little he flaps.
records.identityEvidence: Adult female in fiction. Photograph records do not establish sex or exact adult age.
records.visibleScene: A raven pursues a red-tailed hawk in a clear blue sky.
records.fictionBoundary: The pursuit is source-confirmed. Nest defense, repeated circles and the comparative effort are fiction. The source says raven; the Arches species account identifies its common raven as Corvus corax, consistent with the pictured bird. This taxon match uses park context as well as appearance, not an exact scientific label on the asset.
records.creator: NPS/Martin Tow

records.title: A place for my feet
records.prose: He turned over beneath me. I put my feet out. For a moment there was something to stand on in the sky. Then we let go and went back for each other.
records.holdReason: Hold image: the unusual aerial relationship supports the prose, but the 1977 original has small, soft silhouettes against dull sky. Keep the prose private.

records.fictionBoundary: Aerial interaction and inversion are explicit. Mate relationship, foot contact, release and repeating are fiction; contact is not asserted visible.
